newsitem.title: USA: Consumer groups oppose US meat inspection user fee.
newsitem.headline: Consumer groups oppose US meat inspection user fee.

text.p: U.S. consumer groups said Monday they oppose a Clinton administration proposal to shift most of the cost of federal meat inspection to the meat industry.
In its fiscal 1998 budget, the Clinton administration has proposed $390 million in user fees to cover the cost of putting federal inspectors in meat, poultry and egg plants.

At a public meeting held by the Agriculture Department, consumer groups said the user fee proposal would undermine public confidence in meat inspection and put an unnecessary burden on an industry already implementing major reform.

"We oppose this effort very, very strongly," said Carol Tucker Foreman, former USDA assistant secretary for food safety who heads a coalition of labor unions and consumer groups. "We think the ability of the system to adjust to this kind of change on top of change already out there is likely to bring the whole thing down."
Last year, the government announced an overhaul of the federal meat inspection process which introduced scientific testing for disease-causing bacteria.

USDA said budget constraints make user fees necessary and that preliminary analysis suggests the overall effects will be small. USDA chief economist Keith Collins said the department calculates if the whole cost of user fees was passed on to the consumer it would be a $1.45 increase annually per person.

To implement the proposal, USDA would need authorizing legislation from Congress to be followed by a rulemaking process. USDA officials said legislation had been drafted and would be included in an omnibus bill from the White House to be sent to Capitol Hill in the next few days. Several key lawmakers have indicated they are against user fees.

At the meeting, USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service Administrator Thomas Billy said among the options USDA was considering to assess fees would be user fees based on volume of production or based on hours worked by inspectors.
He also said USDA was looking at an export certificate fee or a fee for incurring extra regulatory costs.
Few industry officials attended the session. Last week, 12 major meat associations sent a joint letter to Billy saying the meeting was "premature" and registering their opposition.
The groups, including the American Meat Institute, the National Broiler Council and the National Pork Producers Council, called the fees a "food tax".

"Given the broad and long-standing opposition to this proposed tax on consumers, livestock producers and the meat and poultry and egg processing industries, we do not believe it is productive to discuss user fee options with FSIS March 10," they wrote in a letter dated March 6.
